profiles.name: Glenn Michael Souther
profiles.description: Glenn Michael Souther was a former U.S. Navy photographer and intelligence specialist with access to sensitive reconnaissance material. A joint Naval Investigative Service and FBI inquiry examined whether he had passed classified information to the Soviet Union. After investigators alerted him to their suspicions, Souther disappeared in May 1986 and reached the Soviet Union. Soviet authorities announced in 1988 that they had granted him asylum and citizenship under the name Mikhail Yevgenyevich Orlov. Soviet reporting after his death in June 1989 acknowledged his intelligence work.

profiles.name: Theodore Branch
profiles.description: Theodore Branch and his wife Cheryl traveled from Pennsylvania to the Soviet Union as tourists in November 1987 and asked to remain. They said Soviet law, order and social equality offered an alternative to capitalism. The Presidium of the Supreme Soviet granted them political asylum in January 1988. The couple worked on English-language radio broadcasts in Moscow. They returned to the United States in September 1988 after less than a year, then asked the Soviet Embassy to let them return when they became dissatisfied with conditions at home; that request was unsuccessful.

profiles.name: Khalfani Malik Khaldun
profiles.description: Khalfani Malik Khaldun, legally Leonard B. McQuay and formerly listed as Khalfani X. Khaldun, is a New Afrikan prison organizer incarcerated in Indiana since 1987. While imprisoned on earlier street offenses, he became a political educator and organizer. Indiana later prosecuted him for the 1994 killing of a prison guard; Khaldun has consistently denied responsibility, and supporters argued that officials singled him out because of his conflicts with prison authorities and organizing. After years of litigation he was convicted and received a sixty-year sentence. A January 2026 federal decision confirms that Khaldun and Leonard McQuay are the same person and that he remains imprisoned; the most recent independently located facility record places him at Westville Correctional Facility.

profiles.name: James “Doc” Holiday
profiles.description: James “Doc” Holiday is a longtime Black liberation and prison organizer associated with the Black Guerrilla Family and the development of Black August commemorations. His political work arose inside prison, rather than from the offense that produced his current sentence. A federal jury convicted Holiday in June 1988 of two counts of possessing cocaine with intent to distribute as part of the Elrader Browning prosecution, and Judge Stephen Wilson sentenced him to life without parole on August 29, 1988. Holiday later spent years in federal supermax custody and continued writing and organizing around Black liberation and prison conditions. A 2023 prisoner-support appeal listed the then-80-year-old Holiday at USP McCreary under federal register number 86555-012.

profiles.name: Howard Spragg
profiles.description: Howard Spragg was one of the eight Union Theological Seminary students known as the "Union Eight" who, on October 16, 1940, the first day of registration under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, collectively refused to register for the draft despite their automatic seminarian exemption. Their joint statement objected to conscription itself: "To us, the war system is an evil part of our social order, and we declare we cannot cooperate with it... We believe that war and conscription are sins against God and humanity." Convicted in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York; sentenced November 14, 1940 to 1 year at FCI Danbury (Connecticut). Most served roughly 9 months before parole. Co-defendants: George Houser, David Dellinger, Don Benedict, Meredith Dallas, Joseph Bevilacqua, Richard Wichlei, William Lovell, Howard Spragg. After release Spragg was ordained in the Congregational Christian Churches and rose to become executive vice president of the United Church Board for Homeland Ministries — the social-action arm of the United Church of Christ — from 1962 to 1981.

profiles.name: Ben Rubin
profiles.description: Ben Rubin was a Communist Party organizer in Reading, Pennsylvania, a wounded Spanish Civil War veteran, and a 1940 congressional candidate. He was repeatedly prosecuted over signatures on Communist Party nominating petitions. An early report incorrectly said he had already received seventeen years; a correction explained that seventeen years was only the possible cumulative exposure. The surviving judgment imposed concurrent terms of one to two years for perjury, while an election-code sentence was suspended. Whether Rubin entered the county prison and how long he remained there are unresolved.

profiles.name: William Weiner
profiles.description: William Weiner was the Communist Party USA’s national treasurer. A federal jury convicted him of using a passport obtained through false statements, and the Supreme Court upheld the conviction in 1941. Although sentenced to two years in federal prison, he never served the sentence because of a serious heart condition.
